Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A collection letter violates the FDCPA when the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it in two or more ways, one of which is inaccurate.

Congress enacted the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to eliminate abusive collection practices and to protect consumers from false and misleading representations. 15 U.S.C. § 1692(e). Section 1692e prohibits "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt," *id.* § 1692e, including "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt," *id.* § 1692e(10). Because the statute is remedial, this Court construes it broadly to give effect to its purpose. *See Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453–54 (3d Cir. 2006); *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 996–97 (3d Cir. 2011).

To decide whether a communication is false, deceptive, or misleading, this Court asks how it would be understood by the "least sophisticated debtor." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000); *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298 (3d Cir. 2008). That objective standard protects "the gullible as well as the shrewd," and it ensures that the FDCPA protects all consumers, including the naive and the trusting, from deceptive practices. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 453–54; *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008). It is also a low standard. It presumes only "a basic level of understanding and willingness to read with care." *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *see also Lesher*, 650 F.3d at 997. It is not a standard that asks whether a reasonable, sophisticated, or legally trained reader could have worked out the correct meaning.

Applying that standard, this Court has held that a collection letter is deceptive "when it can reasonably be read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455 (quotation omitted); *accord Campuzano-Burgos*, 550 F.3d at 298–99. The test does not require the debtor to prove that the collector intended to deceive, or that the debtor was in fact misled. The question is whether the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably adopt the inaccurate reading. If so, the letter violates § 1692e, whatever other, accurate reading the collector says was intended.

This rule follows from the text and purpose of the statute. An ambiguous letter puts the debtor in an impossible position. The debtor must guess which meaning is correct, and the cost of guessing wrong falls on the debtor, who may pay a debt not owed, pay more than is owed, or forgo rights. The collector controls the drafting and can easily avoid the problem by writing clearly. The statute puts the burden of clarity on the collector. A collector that chooses language capable of an inaccurate reading bears the risk of that choice.

The rule has limits, and they confirm that it is applied with care. The least sophisticated debtor is still expected to read a notice in its entirety, and this Court will not credit "bizarre or idiosyncratic" interpretations. *See Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55; *Campuzano-Burgos*, 550 F.3d at 298–99; *Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 147–48 (3d Cir. 2013). Nor does every misstatement create liability. The false or misleading statement must be material, meaning it must be capable of affecting the least sophisticated debtor's decision about how to respond to the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 417–21 (3d Cir. 2015). Where those requirements are met, as they are here, the *Brown* rule governs. *See also Tatis v. Allied Interstate, LLC*, 882 F.3d 422, 426–27 (3d Cir. 2018) (applying the least-sophisticated-debtor standard to determine whether a collection letter was misleading).

### II. Defendant's letter can reasonably be read in an inaccurate way, and the inaccurate reading is material.

[Insert application: (1) quote the operative language; (2) identify the accurate reading the collector will advance; (3) identify the inaccurate reading a least sophisticated debtor could reasonably adopt, and explain why it is not bizarre or idiosyncratic given the letter as a whole; (4) explain why the inaccurate reading is material under *Jensen*, for example because it bears on the amount owed, the debtor's rights, or the consequences of nonpayment.]

Because the letter can reasonably be read in two ways, one of which is inaccurate, and because that inaccuracy is material, Defendant violated 15 U.S.C. § 1692e and § 1692e(10). This Court should reverse.
